title: Κυδοιμός
titleEn: The Twins of Pherae and the Coming of Ares — Iliad 5.519–626
part: The Twins of Pherae and the Coming of Ares (5.519–626)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The two Ajaxes, Odysseus and Diomedes keep the Danaans standing against the Trojan onset like windless clouds on the mountains, and Agamemnon goes through the ranks bidding them respect one another; he then hits Deicoon, the companion of Aeneas, through his shield and belly. Aeneas in turn kills Crethon and Orsilochus, the twin sons of Diocles of Pherae, whose family goes back to the river Alpheus; they had sailed to Troy to win honour for the sons of Atreus, and they fall like young lions killed by men, like high firs. Ares urges on Menelaus, who goes against Aeneas with Antilochus at his side; Aeneas gives way, the dead are dragged off, and Menelaus and Antilochus kill Pylaemenes, leader of the Paphlagonians, and the charioteer Mydon. Then Hector rushes on with Ares and Enyo among the Trojans, and Diomedes shudders and tells his men to withdraw facing the enemy and not to fight a god. Hector kills Menesthes and Anchialus, and Telamonian Ajax kills Amphius but cannot strip him, and gives ground before the Trojan spears.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ Αἴαντε δύω καὶ Ὀδυσσεὺς καὶ Διομήδης
ὄτρυνον Δαναοὺς πολεμιζέμεν·
sentences.tr:
tous d’ Aiante dyō kai Odysseus kai Diomēdēs
otrynon Danaous polemizemen·
sentences.l:
And them the two Ajaxes and Odysseus and Diomedes
urged on, the Danaans, to wage war;
sentences.i: The two Ajaxes, Odysseus and Diomedes urged the Danaans on to wage war;
sentences.n: τοὺς is the article used as a pronoun, ‘them’, and Δαναούς, in apposition, says who they are. Αἴαντε is a dual, ‘the two Ajaxes’, with δύω ‘two’ added; this part names only Telamonian Ajax (at 610), and the other is the son of Oileus. ὄτρυνον is an unaugmented imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, and πολεμιζέμεν the epic infinitive in -έμεν (= Attic πολεμίζειν) of πολεμίζω ‘wage war’. Δαναοί is one of the poem’s three names for the army, and each is kept as the poet chose it.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ
οὔτε βίας Τρώων ὑπεδείδισαν οὔτε ἰωκάς,
sentences.tr:
hoi de kai autoi
oute bias Trōōn hypedeidisan oute iōkas,
sentences.l:
and they themselves too
neither the might of the Trojans feared, nor onsets,
sentences.i: and they themselves, too, were afraid neither of the might of the Trojans nor of their onsets,
sentences.n: οἳ δὲ καὶ αὐτοί is ‘and they themselves too’, the Danaans, and οὔτε … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’. βίας is the accusative plural of βίη ‘might’. ἰωκάς (from ἰωκή) is a rare word whose sense is not certain: perhaps the din of battle (from ἰωή ‘cry’), perhaps the rush of an attack; the translation takes ‘onsets’. ὑπεδείδισαν is an aorist of ὑποδείδω ‘fear’, with ὑπο- adding the sense of shrinking back.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔμενον νεφέλῃσιν ἐοικότες ἅς τε Κρονίων
νηνεμίης ἔστησεν ἐπ’ ἀκροπόλοισιν ὄρεσσιν
ἀτρέμας,
sentences.tr:
all’ emenon nephelēisin eoikotes has te Kroniōn
nēnemiēs estēsen ep’ akropoloisin oressin
atremas,
sentences.l:
but they stood fast, like to clouds which the son of Cronus
in windlessness set upon high mountains
motionless,
sentences.i: but they stood firm, like clouds that the son of Cronus, when no wind blows, sets motionless on the high mountains,
sentences.n: ἔμενον is the imperfect of μένω, here ‘stood fast’. νεφέλῃσιν ἐοικότες ‘like clouds’: ἐοικότες is the perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’, which takes the dative (epic -ῃσιν). The simile runs through the next unit. ἅς τε is the relative with epic τε, and Κρονίων ‘the son of Cronus’ is Zeus, who is not named. ἔστησεν is an aorist that in a simile states what happens whenever the conditions hold, so the English layer puts it in the present. νηνεμίης ‘in windlessness’ is a genitive of the circumstance, and ἀκροπόλοισιν ‘high’ is a dative plural of the adjective ἀκρόπολος ‘on the heights’, built on ἄκρος ‘top’ with a second part of uncertain origin; the Odyssey has the same two words, and its English ‘high mountains’ is kept. ἀτρέμας is the adverb ‘without trembling, motionless’.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ εὕδῃσι μένος Βορέαο καὶ ἄλλων
ζαχρειῶν ἀνέμων, οἵ τε νέφεα σκιόεντα
πνοιῇσιν λιγυρῇσι διασκιδνᾶσιν ἀέντες·
sentences.tr:
ophr’ heudēisi menos Boreao kai allōn
zachreiōn anemōn, hoi te nephea skioenta
pnoiēisin ligyrēisi diaskidnasin aentes·
sentences.i: while the might of the North Wind sleeps, and that of the other very violent winds that scatter the shadowy clouds with their clear-sounding breath as they blow;
sentences.n: ὄφρα with the epic subjunctive εὕδῃσι (= εὕδῃ, from εὕδω ‘sleep’) is ‘so long as … sleeps’. μένος Βορέαο ‘the might of the North Wind’ is a periphrasis for the wind itself (Βορέαο has the epic genitive -αο). ζαχρειῶν ‘very violent’: ζα- is ‘very’, and the rest of the word is of uncertain origin, so the sense is the traditional one. οἵ τε ‘which’ is the relative with epic τε, a general statement; νέφεα is the epic uncontracted plural of νέφος ‘cloud’, and σκιόεντα ‘shadowy’. πνοιῇσιν λιγυρῇσι ‘with clear breaths’ has epic datives in -ῃσιν; λιγυρός ‘clear-sounding’ is the adjective that the Odyssey uses of song. διασκιδνᾶσιν is a present of the verb ‘scatter’ (σκίδνημι with διά), and ἀέντες is the participle of ἄημι ‘blow’.

sentences.t: ὣς Δαναοὶ Τρῶας μένον ἔμπεδον οὐδὲ φέβοντο.
sentences.tr: hōs Danaoi Trōas menon empedon oude phebonto.
sentences.l: So the Danaans awaited the Trojans firmly, nor took flight.
sentences.i: So the Danaans awaited the Trojans steadily, and did not take flight.
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ closes the simile. μένον is the unaugmented imperfect of μένω, here with an object, ‘awaited’ (without one, as in 522, it is ‘stood fast’). ἔμπεδον is the adverb of ἔμπεδος ‘firm’. φέβοντο is the imperfect middle of φέβομαι ‘take flight’, and οὐδέ ‘and … not’.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ἀν’ ὅμιλον ἐφοίτα πολλὰ κελεύων·
sentences.tr: Atreïdēs d’ an’ homilon ephoita polla keleuōn·
sentences.l: And Atreus’-son through the throng went to and fro, bidding much:
sentences.i: The son of Atreus went to and fro through the throng, giving many orders:
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’ is Agamemnon, who speaks in the next unit; the edition prints no quotation marks. ἐφοίτα ‘went to and fro’ is the imperfect of φοιτάω, and ἀν’ ὅμιλον ‘through the throng’ is ἀνά with the accusative. πολλὰ κελεύων ‘bidding much’ is the participle of κελεύω ‘bid’, with πολλά as an adverbial accusative. The first half of the line is also said of Menelaus at 3.449.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι ἀνέρες ἔστε καὶ ἄλκιμον ἦτορ ἕλεσθε,
ἀλλήλους τ’ αἰδεῖσθε κατὰ κρατερὰς ὑσμίνας·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi aneres este kai alkimon ētor helesthe,
allēlous t’ aideisthe kata krateras hysminas·
sentences.l:
“Friends, be men, and take a valiant heart,
and respect one another through the strong battles;
sentences.i: “Friends, be men, and take a valiant heart, and respect one another throughout the strong battles;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι is the vocative, ‘friends’. ἀνέρες ἔστε ‘be men’ has the epic ἀνέρες (nominative plural of ἀνήρ) and the imperative ἔστε of εἰμί. ἄλκιμον ἦτορ ἕλεσθε ‘take a valiant heart’: ἕλεσθε is the aorist imperative middle of αἱρέω, ‘take for yourselves’, and ἦτορ is the heart as the seat of courage. ἀλλήλους τ’ αἰδεῖσθε ‘and respect one another’ is the imperative of αἰδέομαι, which can also mean ‘feel shame’; the next line says what the respect is worth. κρατερὰς ὑσμίνας ‘strong battles’ is a stock phrase, translated every time.

sentences.t: αἰδομένων ἀνδρῶν πλέονες σόοι ἠὲ πέφανται·
sentences.tr: aidomenōn andrōn pleones sooi ēe pephantai·
sentences.l: Of men who feel respect more are safe than have been slain;
sentences.i: Of men who feel respect, more are safe than are slain;
sentences.n: αἰδομένων ἀνδρῶν ‘of men who feel respect’ is a genitive of the group from which the count is made, with αἰδομένων the present participle of αἰδέομαι (the same verb as the imperative before). πλέονες is the epic form of πλείονες ‘more’, and σόοι is the epic form of σῶς ‘safe’. ἠέ ‘than’ follows the comparative; πέφανται is the perfect passive of φένω ‘slay’, ‘have been slain’, a different word from φαίνω ‘show’.

sentences.t: φευγόντων δ’ οὔτ’ ἂρ κλέος ὄρνυται οὔτε τις ἀλκή.
sentences.tr: pheugontōn d’ out’ ar kleos ornytai oute tis alkē.
sentences.l: but of men who flee neither glory arises, nor any might.”
sentences.i: but when men flee, no glory rises up for them, nor any might.”
sentences.n: φευγόντων ‘of men who flee’ is a genitive in the same pattern as the unit before, now for the opposite outcome. οὔτ’ ἂρ … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’. ὄρνυται is the present middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, ‘arises’, and ἀλκή is the strength to defend oneself, ‘might’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ ἀκόντισε δουρὶ θοῶς, βάλε δὲ πρόμον ἄνδρα
Αἰνείω ἕταρον μεγαθύμου Δηϊκόωντα
Περγασίδην, ὃν Τρῶες ὁμῶς Πριάμοιο τέκεσσι
τῖον, ἐπεὶ θοὸς ἔσκε μετὰ πρώτοισι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
ē kai akontise douri thoōs, bale de promon andra
Aineiō hetaron megathymou Dēïkoōnta
Pergasidēn, hon Trōes homōs Priamoio tekessi
tion, epei thoos eske meta prōtoisi machesthai.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and cast with a spear swiftly, and hit a foremost man,
the companion of great-hearted Aeneas, Deicoon,
Pergasus’-son, whom the Trojans equally with Priam’s children
honoured, since he was swift to fight among the first.
sentences.i: So he said, and swiftly cast his spear and hit Deicoon, son of Pergasus, a foremost fighter and the companion of great-hearted Aeneas, whom the Trojans honoured equally with the children of Priam, because he was swift to fight among the foremost.
sentences.n: ἦ καί closes Agamemnon’s speech and starts the action; ἀκόντισε ‘cast’ has no object of its own, and δουρί ‘with a spear’ says what he cast. θοῶς is ‘swiftly’. πρόμον ἄνδρα ‘a foremost man’ is one who stands in the front rank (πρόμος, the word behind πρόμαχοι ‘front-fighters’). Αἰνείω is the epic genitive of Αἰνείας (= Αἰνείαο), agreeing with μεγαθύμου, and ἕταρον is ‘companion’, so ‘the companion of great-hearted Aeneas’; Δηϊκόωντα ‘Deicoon’ is the object of βάλε, with Περγασίδην, a patronymic, ‘son of Pergasus’. ὃν … τῖον is ‘whom they honoured’ (τίω), and ὁμῶς Πριάμοιο τέκεσσι ‘equally with the children of Priam’ has the epic dative plural -εσσι. ἔσκε is the iterative past of εἰμί, used here as a plain ‘was’. μεγαθύμου ‘great-hearted’ is a stock epithet, and θοός ‘swift’ is another.

sentences.t: τόν ῥα κατ’ ἀσπίδα δουρὶ βάλε κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: ton rha kat’ aspida douri bale kreiōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: Him then on the shield with a spear hit lord Agamemnon;
sentences.i: Lord Agamemnon hit him on the shield with his spear;
sentences.n: τόν ῥα ‘him, then’ is Deicoon. βάλλω of a weapon is ‘hit’, and κατ’ ἀσπίδα is ‘on the shield’; the next unit says what the shield did. κρείων ‘ruling’ is translated ‘lord’ and goes with Ἀγαμέμνων as a stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ οὐκ ἔγχος ἔρυτο, διὰ πρὸ δὲ εἴσατο χαλκός,
νειαίρῃ δ’ ἐν γαστρὶ διὰ ζωστῆρος ἔλασσε·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ ouk enchos eryto, dia pro de eisato chalkos,
neiairēi d’ en gastri dia zōstēros elasse·
sentences.l:
and it did not guard against the spear, but right through rushed the bronze,
and in the lower belly through the belt drove it;
sentences.i: but the shield did not keep the spear out: the bronze sped right through it, and he drove the spear through the belt into the lower belly;
sentences.n: ἣ is the feminine article used as a pronoun, ‘it’, the shield (ἀσπίς). ἔρυτο is from ἐρύομαι ‘guard, ward off’, with ἔγχος ‘spear’ as the thing warded off. διὰ … πρό is διαπρό ‘right through’, and εἴσατο is an aorist middle of ἵημι, ‘rushed, sped’; χαλκός ‘bronze’ stands for the spear-point. νειαίρῃ ‘lower’ (literally ‘lowest’) agrees with γαστρί ‘belly’, and ζωστήρ is the belt. ἔλασσε is the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, with Agamemnon as the unstated subject and the spear as the unstated object.

sentences.t: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, ἀράβησε δὲ τεύχε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr: doupēsen de pesōn, arabēse de teuche’ ep’ autōi.
sentences.l: and he fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.i: and he fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.n: δούπησεν ‘fell with a thud’ and ἀράβησε ‘clattered’ are sound-words (aorists of δουπέω and ἀραβέω); τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour’ with the final vowel elided. The line is a formula for a warrior’s fall and stands also at 4.504 and 5.42, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ Αἰνείας Δαναῶν ἕλεν ἄνδρας ἀρίστους
υἷε Διοκλῆος Κρήθωνά τε Ὀρσίλοχόν τε,
sentences.tr:
enth’ aut’ Aineias Danaōn helen andras aristous
huie Dioklēos Krēthōna te Orsilochon te,
sentences.l:
Then in turn Aeneas took of the Danaans the best men,
the two sons of Diocles, Crethon and Orsilochus,
sentences.i: Then, in his turn, Aeneas killed two of the Danaans’ best men, the sons of Diocles, Crethon and Orsilochus,
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ‘then in turn’ answers Agamemnon’s kill with a Trojan one. ἕλεν is the unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω, ‘took’, that is, killed. ἄνδρας ἀρίστους ‘best men’ is explained by the apposition that follows: υἷε is a dual (= υἱέε), ‘the two sons’, so the translation says ‘two of’; Διοκλῆος is the epic genitive of Διοκλῆς, and Κρήθωνα and Ὀρσίλοχον are the two names. Δαναῶν is ‘of the Danaans’.

sentences.t:
τῶν ῥα πατὴρ μὲν ἔναιεν ἐϋκτιμένῃ ἐνὶ Φηρῇ
ἀφνειὸς βιότοιο, γένος δ’ ἦν ἐκ ποταμοῖο
Ἀλφειοῦ, ὅς τ’ εὐρὺ ῥέει Πυλίων διὰ γαίης,
ὃς τέκετ’ Ὀρτίλοχον πολέεσσ’ ἄνδρεσσιν ἄνακτα·
sentences.tr:
tōn rha patēr men enaien eÿktimenēi eni Phērēi
aphneios biotoio, genos d’ ēn ek potamoio
Alpheiou, hos t’ eury rheei Pyliōn dia gaiēs,
hos teket’ Ortilochon poleess’ andressin anakta·
sentences.l:
of whom the father dwelt in well-built Pherae,
rich in livelihood, and the family was from the river
Alpheus, who broadly flows through the land of the Pylians,
who begot Ortilochus, a lord to many men;
sentences.i: Their father lived in well-built Pherae, rich in livelihood, and his family was from the river Alpheus, which flows broadly through the land of the Pylians; and Alpheus begot Ortilochus, a lord over many men;
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of whom’ is the two brothers. ἔναιεν is the imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’; ἐϋκτιμένῃ ‘well-built’ (the edition prints the diaeresis) is the stock epithet of towns, with Φηρῇ the dative of the town Pherae. ἀφνειὸς βιότοιο ‘rich in livelihood’ has a genitive of respect; βίοτος is ‘livelihood, means of living’, distinct from βίος ‘life’. γένος δ’ ἦν ἐκ ποταμοῖο Ἀλφειοῦ says that the family came from the river Alpheus, which is also a god, for ὃς τέκετ’ Ὀρτίλοχον is ‘who begot Ortilochus’ (τέκετ’ the unaugmented aorist of τίκτω). εὐρύ is an adverb, ‘broadly’, and ῥέει is the uncontracted ‘flows’; Πυλίων … γαίης is ‘the land of the Pylians’. ἄνακτα ‘lord’ is in apposition to Ὀρτίλοχον, and πολέεσσ’ ἄνδρεσσιν is the epic dative plural, ‘over many men’. The Odyssey names the same house: ‘to Pherae … the house of Diocles, son of Ortilochus, whom Alpheus begot’ (Odyssey 3.488–489).

sentences.t:
Ὀρτίλοχος δ’ ἄρ’ ἔτικτε Διοκλῆα μεγάθυμον,
ἐκ δὲ Διοκλῆος διδυμάονε παῖδε γενέσθην,
Κρήθων Ὀρσίλοχός τε μάχης εὖ εἰδότε πάσης.
sentences.tr:
Ortilochos d’ ar’ etikte Dioklēa megathymon,
ek de Dioklēos didymaone paide genesthēn,
Krēthōn Orsilochos te machēs eu eidote pasēs.
sentences.l:
And Ortilochus begot great-hearted Diocles,
and from Diocles twin sons were born,
Crethon and Orsilochus, knowing all fighting well.
sentences.i: Ortilochus begot great-hearted Diocles, and from Diocles twin sons were born, Crethon and Orsilochus, who both knew all fighting well.
sentences.n: The family tree runs Alpheus, Ortilochus, Diocles, and then the twins. ἔτικτε is the imperfect of τίκτω, said of a father ‘begot’. ἐκ δὲ Διοκλῆος … γενέσθην is ‘and from Diocles … were born’, γενέσθην the dual aorist of γίγνομαι, and διδυμάονε παῖδε ‘twin sons’ are duals too. εὖ εἰδότε μάχης πάσης ‘knowing all fighting well’: εἰδότε is the dual perfect participle of οἶδα, with the genitive of what is known. μεγάθυμον ‘great-hearted’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
τὼ μὲν ἄρ’ ἡβήσαντε μελαινάων ἐπὶ νηῶν
Ἴλιον εἰς εὔπωλον ἅμ’ Ἀργείοισιν ἑπέσθην,
τιμὴν Ἀτρεΐδῃς Ἀγαμέμνονι καὶ Μενελάῳ
ἀρνυμένω·
sentences.tr:
tō men ar’ hēbēsante melainaōn epi nēōn
Ilion eis eupōlon ham’ Argeioisin hepesthēn,
timēn Atreïdēis Agamemnoni kai Menelaōi
arnymenō·
sentences.l:
The two, then, having come to manhood, on black ships
to Ilium of the fine foals along with the Argives followed,
honour for Atreus’-sons, Agamemnon and Menelaus,
winning;
sentences.i: The two of them, when they had come to manhood, followed along with the Argives in black ships to Ilium of the fine foals, winning honour for the sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus;
sentences.n: The verb and the participles here are duals: ἡβήσαντε ‘having come to manhood’, ἑπέσθην ‘followed’ (ἕπομαι) and ἀρνυμένω ‘winning’, all agreeing with τὼ ‘the two’. μελαινάων ἐπὶ νηῶν ‘on black ships’ has the epic genitive plural -άων. Ἴλιον εἰς εὔπωλον ‘to Ilium of the fine foals’ is the Odyssey’s phrase for Troy, εὔπωλος meaning ‘with fine horses’; Ἀργείοισιν is ‘the Argives’, the third of the poem’s names for the army. τιμὴν … ἀρνυμένω ‘winning honour’ means winning the satisfaction owed for the wrong done to the Atreidae. Ἀτρεΐδῃς is an epic dative, here ‘for the sons of Atreus’, and Ἀγαμέμνονι καὶ Μενελάῳ are in apposition.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ αὖθι τέλος θανάτοιο κάλυψεν.
sentences.tr: tō d’ authi telos thanatoio kalypsen.
sentences.l: and the two of them, there, the end of death covered.
sentences.i: but there the end that death brings covered the two of them.
sentences.n: τὼ δ’ is the pair again, and αὖθι is ‘there, on the spot’. τέλος θανάτοιο is ‘the end of death’, and κάλυψεν ‘covered’ is the verb that is also used of darkness covering a man’s eyes.

sentences.t:
οἵω τώ γε λέοντε δύω ὄρεος κορυφῇσιν
ἐτραφέτην ὑπὸ μητρὶ βαθείης τάρφεσιν ὕλης·
sentences.tr:
hoiō tō ge leonte dyō oreos koryphēisin
etraphetēn hypo mētri batheiēs tarphesin hylēs·
sentences.l:
Such as those two lions, a pair, that on a mountain’s peaks
were reared beneath their mother in the thickets of a deep wood;
sentences.i: Like two lions that were reared on a mountain’s peaks beneath their mother, in the thickets of a deep wood;
sentences.n: A new simile for the twin brothers. οἵω is a dual, ‘such as’, which the τοίω of 559 answers (‘such were’). τώ γε λέοντε δύω is ‘those two lions, a pair’, with the duals τώ and λέοντε. ὄρεος is the epic genitive of ὄρος ‘mountain’, and κορυφῇσιν the epic dative plural of κορυφή ‘peak’. ἐτραφέτην is the dual aorist passive of τρέφω ‘were reared’, ὑπὸ μητρί ‘beneath their mother’ with the dative, and βαθείης ὕλης τάρφεσιν ‘in the thickets of a deep wood’ (τάρφος ‘thicket’, epic dative plural).

sentences.t:
τὼ μὲν ἄρ’ ἁρπάζοντε βόας καὶ ἴφια μῆλα
σταθμοὺς ἀνθρώπων κεραΐζετον, ὄφρα καὶ αὐτὼ
ἀνδρῶν ἐν παλάμῃσι κατέκταθεν ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ·
sentences.tr:
tō men ar’ harpazonte boas kai iphia mēla
stathmous anthrōpōn keraïzeton, ophra kai autō
andrōn en palamēisi katektathen oxeï chalkōi·
sentences.i: These two seized cattle and stout flocks and ravaged the steadings of men, until they themselves, too, were killed at the hands of men with sharp bronze;
sentences.n: ἁρπάζοντε and κεραΐζετον are duals, ‘seizing’ and ‘ravaged’ (κεραΐζω ‘ravage’, an imperfect). σταθμούς ‘steadings’ are the farm-buildings where stock is kept, and ἴφια μῆλα ‘stout flocks’ is the Odyssey’s phrase. ὄφρα καὶ αὐτώ is ‘until they themselves too’, and κατέκταθεν is the aorist passive of κατακτείνω in the old form -θεν for -θησαν, ‘were killed’ (a plural verb after the dual αὐτώ). ἐν παλάμῃσι ‘in the hands of’ means ‘at the hands of’, and ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ is ‘sharp bronze’.

sentences.t:
τοίω τὼ χείρεσσιν ὑπ’ Αἰνείαο δαμέντε
καππεσέτην, ἐλάτῃσιν ἐοικότες ὑψηλῇσι.
sentences.tr:
toiō tō cheiressin hyp’ Aineiao damente
kappesetēn, elatēisin eoikotes hypsēlēisi.
sentences.l:
such, those two, by the hands of Aeneas subdued,
fell down, like to high firs.
sentences.i: Such were the two who, overcome by the hands of Aeneas, fell down like high firs.
sentences.n: τοίω τὼ ‘such, those two’ answers οἵω in 554 and closes the simile. δαμέντε is the dual aorist passive participle of δάμνημι ‘subdue’, with χείρεσσιν ὑπ’ Αἰνείαο ‘by the hands of Aeneas’ (epic genitive -αο). καππεσέτην is the dual of κατέπεσον ‘fell down’, with κατ- assimilated before π. ἐλάτῃσιν ἐοικότες ‘like firs’ has ἐοικότες in the masculine plural though the subject is a dual; ὑψηλῇσι is ‘high’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ πεσόντ’ ἐλέησεν ἀρηΐφιλος Μενέλαος,
βῆ δὲ διὰ προμάχων κεκορυθμένος αἴθοπι χαλκῷ
σείων ἐγχείην·
sentences.tr:
tō de pesont’ eleēsen arēïphilos Menelaos,
bē de dia promachōn kekorythmenos aithopi chalkōi
seiōn encheiēn·
sentences.i: Menelaus, dear to Ares, pitied the two as they fell; and he went through the foremost fighters, armed with bronze that has the look of fire, shaking his spear;
sentences.n: τὼ δὲ πεσόντ’ is ‘and the two, fallen’ (πεσόντε, the dual aorist participle of πίπτω), the object of ἐλέησεν ‘pitied’. ἀρηΐφιλος ‘dear to Ares’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet, and the god it names comes in the next unit. βῆ δὲ διὰ προμάχων κεκορυθμένος αἴθοπι χαλκῷ is a formula (it stands also at 4.495), and its English is kept: προμάχων ‘front-fighters’, and κεκορυθμένος is the perfect passive participle of κορύσσω ‘arm’ (from κόρυς ‘helmet’); αἴθοπι χαλκῷ ‘fire-faced bronze’ is αἴθω ‘burn’ with ὄψ ‘face’. σείων ἐγχείην is ‘shaking his spear’.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ὄτρυνεν μένος Ἄρης,
τὰ φρονέων ἵνα χερσὶν ὑπ’ Αἰνείαο δαμείη.
sentences.tr:
tou d’ otrynen menos Arēs,
ta phroneōn hina chersin hyp’ Aineiao dameiē.
sentences.l:
and his might Ares urged on,
thinking this, that by the hands of Aeneas he might be subdued.
sentences.i: and Ares urged on his might, intending that he should be overcome by the hands of Aeneas.
sentences.n: τοῦ is the possessive genitive ‘his’ (Menelaus), with μένος ‘might’ as the object of ὄτρυνεν, an unaugmented imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’. Ares acts for the Trojans, whom he leads at 592. τὰ φρονέων is ‘thinking these things, with this purpose’, and ἵνα with the optative δαμείη (the passive aorist of δάμνημι) is ‘that he might be subdued’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἴδεν Ἀντίλοχος μεγαθύμου Νέστορος υἱός,
βῆ δὲ διὰ προμάχων·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ iden Antilochos megathymou Nestoros huios,
bē de dia promachōn·
sentences.l:
And him saw Antilochus, great-hearted Nestor’s son,
and went through the front-fighters;
sentences.i: Antilochus, the son of great-hearted Nestor, saw him, and went through the foremost fighters;
sentences.n: τὸν is Menelaus, and ἴδεν the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω. Ἀντίλοχος … Νέστορος υἱός is ‘Antilochus, Nestor’s son’, with μεγαθύμου ‘great-hearted’ the stock epithet of Nestor here. βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω, and διὰ προμάχων is ‘through the front-fighters’, as at 562.

sentences.t:
περὶ γὰρ δίε ποιμένι λαῶν
μή τι πάθοι, μέγα δέ σφας ἀποσφήλειε πόνοιο.
sentences.tr:
peri gar die poimeni laōn
mē ti pathoi, mega de sphas aposphēleie ponoio.
sentences.l:
for he feared exceedingly for the shepherd of the people
lest he suffer something, and greatly make them fall short of toil.
sentences.i: for he was greatly afraid for the shepherd of the people, lest he come to some harm and rob them, greatly, of the fruit of their toil.
sentences.n: περὶ γὰρ δίε: περί is an adverb, ‘exceedingly’, and δίε is an epic imperfect ‘feared’, from δίω, a by-form of δείδω ‘fear’, taking the dative ποιμένι λαῶν ‘for the shepherd of the people’, who is Menelaus. μή τι πάθοι is ‘lest he suffer something’, μή with the aorist optative of πάσχω in a fear clause. ἀποσφήλειε is the aorist optative of ἀποσφάλλω ‘make fall short’, with the genitive πόνοιο ‘of toil’ for what they miss; σφας is ‘them’, the Achaeans. The translation supplies ‘the fruit of’: Menelaus’ death would make all their labour vain.

sentences.t:
τὼ μὲν δὴ χεῖράς τε καὶ ἔγχεα ὀξυόεντα
ἀντίον ἀλλήλων ἐχέτην μεμαῶτε μάχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
tō men dē cheiras te kai enchea oxyoenta
antion allēlōn echetēn memaōte machesthai·
sentences.l:
Those two now both hands and sharp spears
against one another held, eager to fight;
sentences.i: The two of them held out their hands and sharp spears against one another, eager to fight;
sentences.n: τὼ μὲν δή ‘those two now’ is Menelaus and Aeneas, now face to face; the verb ἐχέτην and the participle μεμαῶτε are duals (ἔχω ‘hold’, and μεμαώς ‘eager’, the perfect participle of μάω ‘strive’, perfect μέμαα). ἔγχεα ὀξυόεντα ‘sharp spears’ is the Odyssey’s phrase. ἀντίον ἀλλήλων is ‘against one another’, and μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ is an infinitive of purpose after ‘eager’.

sentences.t: Ἀντίλοχος δὲ μάλ’ ἄγχι παρίστατο ποιμένι λαῶν.
sentences.tr: Antilochos de mal’ anchi paristato poimeni laōn.
sentences.l: and Antilochus very near stood beside the shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: and Antilochus took his stand very close beside the shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: Ἀντίλοχος is the subject, and παρίστατο ‘stood beside’ is the imperfect of παρίσταμαι. ποιμένι λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is Menelaus again, in the dative. μάλ’ ἄγχι is ‘very near’.

sentences.t:
Αἰνείας δ’ οὐ μεῖνε θοός περ ἐὼν πολεμιστὴς
ὡς εἶδεν δύο φῶτε παρ’ ἀλλήλοισι μένοντε.
sentences.tr:
Aineias d’ ou meine thoos per eōn polemistēs
hōs eiden dyo phōte par’ allēloisi menonte.
sentences.l:
And Aeneas did not stand fast, swift though being a warrior,
when he saw two men beside one another standing fast.
sentences.i: But Aeneas, swift warrior though he was, did not hold his ground when he saw the two men standing firm beside each other.
sentences.n: οὐ μεῖνε ‘did not stand fast’ is the unaugmented aorist of μένω, used without an object: he did not hold his ground. θοός περ ἐὼν πολεμιστής is ‘though a swift warrior’, περ with the participle ἐών meaning ‘though’, and θοός ‘swift’ is a stock epithet that was given to Deicoon at 536. δύο φῶτε is the dual ‘two men’, Menelaus and Antilochus, and μένοντε the dual participle ‘standing fast’ — the same verb as in the negative before.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν νεκροὺς ἔρυσαν μετὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν,
τὼ μὲν ἄρα δειλὼ βαλέτην ἐν χερσὶν ἑταίρων,
αὐτὼ δὲ στρεφθέντε μετὰ πρώτοισι μαχέσθην.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ epei oun nekrous erysan meta laon Achaiōn,
tō men ara deilō baletēn en chersin hetairōn,
autō de strephthente meta prōtoisi machesthēn.
sentences.l:
And they, when then the dead they had dragged to the people of the Achaeans,
the two, then, miserable ones, put in the hands of companions,
but themselves, having turned, fought among the first.
sentences.i: And when they had dragged the dead to the host of the Achaeans, they put the two miserable men into the hands of their companions, and themselves turned and fought among the foremost.
sentences.n: οἳ is Menelaus and Antilochus. ἔρυσαν is an aorist of ἐρύω ‘drag’, and νεκρούς are the two dead sons of Diocles. In τὼ μὲν ἄρα δειλὼ the dual τὼ … δειλώ is ‘the two miserable ones’, the dead, and βαλέτην is the dual aorist of βάλλω in the sense ‘put’, not of a weapon. αὐτὼ δὲ ‘but themselves’ is the two living men again; στρεφθέντε is the dual aorist passive participle of στρέφω ‘turn’, and μαχέσθην a dual form of μάχομαι ‘fight’. Line 574 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the short final syllable of ἄρα stands in the long place of the second foot.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα Πυλαιμένεα ἑλέτην ἀτάλαντον Ἄρηϊ
ἀρχὸν Παφλαγόνων μεγαθύμων ἀσπιστάων.
sentences.tr:
entha Pylaimenea heletēn atalanton Arēï
archon Paphlagonōn megathymōn aspistaōn.
sentences.l:
There Pylaemenes the two took, the equal of Ares,
commander of the great-hearted Paphlagonians, shield-bearers.
sentences.i: There the two of them killed Pylaemenes, the equal of Ares, commander of the great-hearted Paphlagonians, the shield-bearers.
sentences.n: ἑλέτην is the dual aorist of αἱρέω ‘took’, that is, killed, and its subject is Menelaus and Antilochus; the lines that follow share out the work, Menelaus killing Pylaemenes and Antilochus Mydon. Πυλαιμένεα is the accusative of Πυλαιμένης. ἀτάλαντον Ἄρηϊ ‘the equal of Ares’ has the dative of the person compared, and ἀρχὸν Παφλαγόνων μεγαθύμων ἀσπιστάων is ‘commander of the great-hearted Paphlagonians, shield-bearers’ (ἀσπιστής, epic genitive plural -άων). Line 576 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the final syllable of Πυλαιμένεα, short by nature, stands in the long place of the third foot.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ Ἀτρεΐδης δουρικλειτὸς Μενέλαος
ἑσταότ’ ἔγχεϊ νύξε κατὰ κληῗδα τυχήσας·
sentences.tr:
ton men ar’ Atreïdēs dourikleitos Menelaos
hestaot’ encheï nyxe kata klēïda tychēsas·
sentences.l:
Him, then, Atreus’-son, Menelaus famed-for-the-spear,
standing with a spear stabbed at the collar-bone, having hit it;
sentences.i: Menelaus, the son of Atreus, famed for his spear, stabbed him with his spear as he stood, hitting him at the collar-bone;
sentences.n: τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ ‘him, then’ is Pylaemenes. Ἀτρεΐδης δουρικλειτὸς Μενέλαος is ‘Menelaus, son of Atreus, famed for his spear’, δουρικλειτός being δόρυ ‘spear’ with κλειτός ‘famed’, a stock epithet. ἑσταότ’ is the Homeric perfect participle of ἵστημι (= ἑστηκότα), ‘standing’, so he was on his feet when he was stabbed. ἔγχεϊ is the epic dative ‘with a spear’, and νύξε the unaugmented aorist of νύσσω ‘stab’. κατὰ κληῗδα is ‘at the collar-bone’ (the edition prints the diaeresis), and τυχήσας is the aorist participle of τυγχάνω in its sense ‘hit’.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχος δὲ Μύδωνα βάλ’ ἡνίοχον θεράποντα
ἐσθλὸν Ἀτυμνιάδην·
sentences.tr:
Antilochos de Mydōna bal’ hēniochon theraponta
esthlon Atymniadēn·
sentences.l:
and Antilochus hit Mydon, the charioteer, the attendant,
the good one, Atymnius’-son;
sentences.i: and Antilochus hit Mydon, the son of Atymnius, a good charioteer and attendant;
sentences.n: βάλ’ is βάλε ‘hit’. ἡνίοχον θεράποντα ‘charioteer, attendant’ names his two roles (ἡνία ‘reins’ and ἔχω; θεράπων ‘attendant’), ἐσθλόν is ‘good’, and Ἀτυμνιάδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Atymnius’. The Greek does not say whose charioteer he was; after the death of Pylaemenes in the lines above, the natural reading is that he was his.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ὑπέστρεφε μώνυχας ἵππους·
sentences.tr: ho d’ hypestrephe mōnychas hippous·
sentences.l: and he was turning about the solid-hoofed horses;
sentences.i: and he was turning the solid-hoofed horses about;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is ‘and he’, Mydon. ὑπέστρεφε is the imperfect of ὑποστρέφω, here with an object, ‘was turning about’. μώνυχας ἵππους ‘solid-hoofed horses’ is the stock phrase (μώνυξ ‘with an undivided hoof’, the usual explanation).

sentences.t: χερμαδίῳ ἀγκῶνα τυχὼν μέσον·
sentences.tr: chermadiōi ankōna tychōn meson·
sentences.l: with a rock the elbow having hit, in the middle;
sentences.i: hitting him with a rock full on the elbow;
sentences.n: The participle τυχών (the aorist of τυγχάνω ‘hit’) has Antilochus as its subject, and the sentence continues from βάλ’ in 580. χερμαδίῳ ‘with a rock’ is a dative of means (χερμάδιον, a rock that can be thrown by hand), and ἀγκῶνα ‘elbow’ is the accusative of the part struck; μέσον is ‘in the middle’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἄρα χειρῶν
ἡνία λεύκ’ ἐλέφαντι χαμαὶ πέσον ἐν κονίῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
ek d’ ara cheirōn
hēnia leuk’ elephanti chamai peson en koniēisin.
sentences.l:
and out of his hands
the reins, white with ivory, fell to the ground in the dust.
sentences.i: and the reins, white with ivory, fell from his hands to the ground in the dust.
sentences.n: ἐκ … πέσον ‘fell out’ is a split compound, the preverb standing apart; πέσον is the unaugmented aorist of πίπτω, plural to agree with the neuter plural ἡνία ‘reins’. λεύκ’ ἐλέφαντι is ‘white with ivory’, ἐλέφαντι a dative of means; the Greek does not say how the ivory was worked in. χαμαί is ‘to the ground’, and ἐν κονίῃσιν ‘in the dust’ has the plural form of κονίη.

sentences.t: Ἀντίλοχος δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπαΐξας ξίφει ἤλασε κόρσην·
sentences.tr: Antilochos d’ ar’ epaïxas xiphei ēlase korsēn·
sentences.l: and Antilochus, then, rushing on, with a sword struck the side of the head;
sentences.i: Antilochus then rushed in and struck him on the side of the head with his sword;
sentences.n: ἐπαΐξας is the aorist participle of ἐπαΐσσω ‘rush on’. ξίφει is the dative of ξίφος ‘sword’, a dative of means. ἤλασε is from ἐλαύνω, which of a blow is ‘strike’, and κόρσην is ‘the side of the head’ (accusative of the part struck).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἀσθμαίνων εὐεργέος ἔκπεσε δίφρου
κύμβαχος ἐν κονίῃσιν ἐπὶ βρεχμόν τε καὶ ὤμους.
sentences.tr:
autar ho g’ asthmainōn euergeos ekpese diphrou
kymbachos en koniēisin epi brechmon te kai ōmous.
sentences.l:
but he, gasping, out of the well-made chariot fell
head-down in the dust upon the crown of the head and the shoulders.
sentences.i: and he, gasping, fell out of the well-made chariot head first into the dust, on the crown of his head and his shoulders.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ is ‘but he’, Mydon, and ἀσθμαίνων ‘gasping’ is a present participle. εὐεργέος … δίφρου is ‘of the well-made chariot’ (εὐεργής ‘well-wrought’, with the epic genitive -έος), and ἔκπεσε is the unaugmented aorist ‘fell out’. κύμβαχος ‘head-down’ is a rare word, usually taken as ‘head foremost’; its formation is not clear. βρεχμός, also rare, is the top of the head, ‘the crown’ being the usual gloss, though the word may mean the front of the skull. ἐπὶ βρεχμόν τε καὶ ὤμους is ‘upon the crown of the head and the shoulders’, the accusatives naming the parts he landed on.

sentences.t: δηθὰ μάλ’ ἑστήκει·
sentences.tr: dētha mal’ hestēkei·
sentences.l: for a very long time he stood;
sentences.i: He stood there for a very long time;
sentences.n: δηθά is ‘for a long time’, and μάλα ‘very’. ἑστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι with the sense of an imperfect, ‘was standing’. After κύμβαχος the Greek can only mean that he stayed fixed where he had landed, on his head and shoulders in the deep sand named in the next line.

sentences.t: τύχε γάρ ῥ’ ἀμάθοιο βαθείης·
sentences.tr: tyche gar rh’ amathoio batheiēs·
sentences.l: for he had chanced upon deep sand;
sentences.i: for he had come down in deep sand;
sentences.n: τύχε is the unaugmented aorist of τυγχάνω, which with the genitive (ἀμάθοιο) means ‘chance upon, light on’, a different use from the ‘hit’ of τυχών above. ἄμαθος is ‘sand’, as distinct from κονίη ‘dust’, and βαθείης ‘deep’ is the feminine genitive. ῥ’ is the particle ῥα (= ἄρα), ‘then, you see’.

sentences.t: ὄφρ’ ἵππω πλήξαντε χαμαὶ βάλον ἐν κονίῃσι·
sentences.tr: ophr’ hippō plēxante chamai balon en koniēisi·
sentences.l: until the two horses, having struck him, threw him to the ground in the dust;
sentences.i: until the two horses struck him and threw him to the ground in the dust;
sentences.n: ὄφρα here is ‘until’. ἵππω is the dual ‘the two horses’, and πλήξαντε the dual aorist participle of πλήσσω ‘strike’; the Greek gives no object, and the translation supplies ‘him’ for both verbs. βάλον is the aorist of βάλλω in the sense ‘threw down’ (not of a weapon), and χαμαί is ‘to the ground’.

sentences.t: τοὺς ἵμασ’ Ἀντίλοχος, μετὰ δὲ στρατὸν ἤλασ’ Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr: tous himas’ Antilochos, meta de straton ēlas’ Achaiōn.
sentences.l: These Antilochus whipped, and toward the army of the Achaeans drove them.
sentences.i: Antilochus whipped them on and drove them to the army of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: τοὺς is the horses, masculine plural for the pair. ἵμασ’ is ἵμασε, ‘whipped’. ἤλασ’ is ἤλασε, from ἐλαύνω, which of driving horses is ‘drive’ (the same verb is ‘strike’ of the sword blow at 584). μετὰ … στρατόν is ‘to the army’, μετά with the accusative of the goal.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ Ἕκτωρ ἐνόησε κατὰ στίχας, ὦρτο δ’ ἐπ’ αὐτοὺς
κεκλήγων·
sentences.tr:
tous d’ Hektōr enoēse kata stichas, ōrto d’ ep’ autous
keklēgōn·
sentences.l:
And them Hector noticed through the ranks, and rushed upon them
shrieking;
sentences.i: Hector caught sight of them along the ranks and rushed upon them with a shrill cry;
sentences.n: τοὺς is Menelaus and Antilochus. ἐνόησε is the aorist of νοέω, ‘noticed’, and κατὰ στίχας is ‘along the ranks’. ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι, ‘rose, rushed’, with ἐπ’ αὐτούς ‘upon them’. κεκλήγων is the participle of κέκληγα ‘cry sharply’, a word for a shrill, carrying cry.

sentences.t:
ἅμα δὲ Τρώων εἵποντο φάλαγγες
καρτεραί·
sentences.tr:
hama de Trōōn heiponto phalanges
karterai·
sentences.l:
and together followed the battle-lines of the Trojans,
strong ones;
sentences.i: and the strong battle-lines of the Trojans followed along with him;
sentences.n: ἅμα is ‘together’, here with Hector. εἵποντο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, and φάλαγγες are ‘battle-lines’. καρτεραί is the feminine plural of καρτερός ‘strong’, set after its noun for emphasis.

sentences.t:
ἦρχε δ’ ἄρα σφιν Ἄρης καὶ πότνι’ Ἐνυώ,
ἣ μὲν ἔχουσα Κυδοιμὸν ἀναιδέα δηϊοτῆτος,
Ἄρης δ’ ἐν παλάμῃσι πελώριον ἔγχος ἐνώμα,
φοίτα δ’ ἄλλοτε μὲν πρόσθ’ Ἕκτορος, ἄλλοτ’ ὄπισθε.
sentences.tr:
ērche d’ ara sphin Arēs kai potni’ Enyō,
hē men echousa Kydoimon anaidea dēïotētos,
Arēs d’ en palamēisi pelōrion enchos enōma,
phoita d’ allote men prosth’ Hektoros, allot’ opisthe.
sentences.l:
and led them Ares and lady Enyo,
she, for her part, holding the shameless Uproar of fighting,
and Ares in his hands a huge spear wielded,
and he went to and fro, at one time in front of Hector, at another behind.
sentences.i: Ares and lady Enyo led them; she, for her part, held ruthless Uproar of the fighting, and Ares wielded a huge spear in his hands, and he went to and fro, now in front of Hector, now behind.
sentences.n: ἦρχε is the imperfect of ἄρχω ‘lead’, in the singular though it has two subjects (it agrees with the nearer); σφιν is ‘them’, the Trojans. Ἐνυώ is Enyo, a war-goddess, with πότνια ‘lady’. Κυδοιμός ‘Uproar’ is the personified din and confusion of battle, and the English capitalises it as a being, as with ‘Strife’. ἀναιδέα is ‘shameless’ in the literal layer; of a thing that spares nothing the translation says ‘ruthless’, as for the stone at 4.521. δηϊοτῆτος is the genitive of δηϊοτής ‘fighting’. ἐνώμα is the imperfect of νωμάω ‘wield’, with πελώριον ‘huge’ and ἐν παλάμῃσι ‘in his hands’. φοίτα is the imperfect of φοιτάω ‘go to and fro’, and its unstated subject is Ares, the last named; ἄλλοτε μέν … ἄλλοτε is ‘at one time … at another’.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ ἰδὼν ῥίγησε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: ton de idōn rhigēse boēn agathos Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: And him, having seen, shuddered Diomedes, good at the war-cry;
sentences.i: Diomedes, good at the war-cry, shuddered when he saw him;
sentences.n: τὸν is most naturally Ares, whom the unit before has just described, and whom Diomedes names in his speech. ἰδών is the aorist participle of ὁράω, and ῥίγησε the aorist of ῥιγέω ‘shudder’. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is Diomedes’ stock epithet, with βοήν an accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀνὴρ ἀπάλαμνος ἰὼν πολέος πεδίοιο
στήῃ ἐπ’ ὠκυρόῳ ποταμῷ ἅλα δὲ προρέοντι
ἀφρῷ μορμύροντα ἰδών, ἀνά τ’ ἔδραμ’ ὀπίσσω,
ὣς τότε Τυδεΐδης ἀνεχάζετο, εἶπέ τε λαῷ·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ anēr apalamnos iōn poleos pedioio
stēēi ep’ ōkyroōi potamōi hala de proreonti
aphrōi mormyronta idōn, ana t’ edram’ opissō,
hōs tote Tydeïdēs anechazeto, eipe te laōi·
sentences.l:
And as when a man, helpless, going over a wide plain,
stands at a swift-flowing river flowing forth to the sea,
having seen it roaring with foam, and runs back,
so then Tydeus’-son drew back, and said to the people:
sentences.i: As when a helpless man, going over a wide plain, halts at a swift-flowing river that runs on to the sea, and, seeing it roar with foam, runs back, so then the son of Tydeus drew back, and said to the people:
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ opens the simile, ‘and as when’, with the epic subjunctive στήῃ; the aorist ἔδραμε is the general-truth aorist, so the English layer uses the present. ἀπάλαμνος ‘helpless’ is ἀ- with παλάμη ‘hand, device’, a man with no resource. πολέος πεδίοιο is the genitive of the ground crossed, ‘over a wide plain’ (epic genitives -εος, -οιο). ὠκυρόῳ ‘swift-flowing’ is ὠκύς ‘swift’ with ῥόος ‘flow’. The edition prints ἅλα δέ as two words; the sense is ἅλαδε ‘to the sea’ (the -δε of direction), with προρέοντι ‘flowing forth’. μορμύροντα ‘roaring’ agrees with the unstated river, the object of ἰδών, and ἀφρῷ ‘with foam’ is a dative of means. ἀνεχάζετο is the imperfect of ἀναχάζομαι ‘draw back’, Τυδεΐδης is ‘son of Tydeus’ (Diomedes), and εἶπέ τε λαῷ ‘and said to the people’ leads into his speech.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι οἷον δὴ θαυμάζομεν Ἕκτορα δῖον
αἰχμητήν τ’ ἔμεναι καὶ θαρσαλέον πολεμιστήν·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi hoion dē thaumazomen Hektora dion
aichmētēn t’ emenai kai tharsaleon polemistēn·
sentences.l:
“Friends, how greatly indeed we marvel at heavenly Hector
to be a spearman and a bold warrior;
sentences.i: “Friends, how we marvel at heavenly Hector, that he is a spearman and a bold warrior;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι ‘friends’ opens the speech; the edition prints no quotation marks. οἷον δή is exclamatory, ‘how greatly indeed’, with θαυμάζομεν ‘we marvel’ taking the accusative Ἕκτορα and the infinitive ἔμεναι (= εἶναι), ‘we marvel at Hector, that he is’. The next lines undercut the praise: a god is at his side. δῖον ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet, αἰχμητής ‘spearman’, θαρσαλέος ‘bold’, and πολεμιστής ‘warrior’.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ αἰεὶ πάρα εἷς γε θεῶν, ὃς λοιγὸν ἀμύνει·
sentences.tr: tōi d’ aiei para heis ge theōn, hos loigon amynei·
sentences.l: but by him always is one, at least, of the gods, who wards off ruin;
sentences.i: but at his side there is always at least one of the gods, who wards off ruin;
sentences.n: τῷ δ’ is ‘but for him’, and πάρα is πάρεστι ‘is beside’, with the accent on the first syllable. αἰεί is ‘always’, and εἷς γε θεῶν ‘one, at least, of the gods’. ὃς λοιγὸν ἀμύνει is ‘who wards off ruin’, λοιγός being ‘ruin’ and ἀμύνω ‘ward off’.

sentences.t: καὶ νῦν οἱ πάρα κεῖνος Ἄρης βροτῷ ἀνδρὶ ἐοικώς.
sentences.tr: kai nyn hoi para keinos Arēs brotōi andri eoikōs.
sentences.l: and now beside him is that Ares, to a mortal man likened.
sentences.i: and now that Ares is at his side, like a mortal man.
sentences.n: οἱ is the dative ‘him’, Hector, and πάρα again ‘is beside’. κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος ‘that’, pointing: ‘that Ares there’. βροτῷ ἀνδρὶ ἐοικώς is ‘like a mortal man’, ἐοικώς the perfect participle of ἔοικα, as ἐοικότες at 560.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πρὸς Τρῶας τετραμμένοι αἰὲν ὀπίσσω
εἴκετε, μηδὲ θεοῖς μενεαινέμεν ἶφι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
alla pros Trōas tetrammenoi aien opissō
eikete, mēde theois meneainemen iphi machesthai.
sentences.l:
But toward the Trojans turned, always backward
give way, and not to be eager to fight the gods with force.”
sentences.i: But with your faces turned to the Trojans, keep withdrawing backward, and do not be eager to fight the gods powerfully.”
sentences.n: πρὸς Τρῶας τετραμμένοι is ‘turned toward the Trojans’ (τετραμμένοι the perfect passive participle of τρέπω), so they fall back facing the enemy; αἰὲν ὀπίσσω is ‘always backward’. εἴκετε is the plural imperative of εἴκω ‘give way’. μηδὲ … μενεαινέμεν is an infinitive used as an imperative, ‘and do not be eager’, with the epic ending -έμεν (= μενεαίνειν); μάχεσθαι θεοῖς is ‘to fight the gods’, and ἶφι ‘with force’ is an old instrumental form. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, Τρῶες δὲ μάλα σχεδὸν ἤλυθον αὐτῶν.
sentences.tr: hōs ar’ ephē, Trōes de mala schedon ēlython autōn.
sentences.l: So then he spoke, and the Trojans very near them came.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the Trojans came very close to them.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη is ‘so then he spoke’, ἔφη the imperfect of φημί; this is the standing formula that closes a speech. ἤλυθον is the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι (= ἦλθον), and σχεδόν ‘near’ takes the genitive αὐτῶν ‘them’, with μάλα ‘very’. A new paragraph begins here in the edition.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ Ἕκτωρ δύο φῶτε κατέκτανεν εἰδότε χάρμης
εἰν ἑνὶ δίφρῳ ἐόντε, Μενέσθην Ἀγχίαλόν τε.
sentences.tr:
enth’ Hektōr dyo phōte katektanen eidote charmēs
ein heni diphrōi eonte, Menesthēn Anchialon te.
sentences.l:
There Hector two men killed, knowing the joy of battle,
in one chariot being, Menesthes and Anchialus.
sentences.i: There Hector killed two men who knew the joy of battle, both in one chariot, Menesthes and Anchialus.
sentences.n: κατέκτανεν is the aorist of κατακτείνω ‘kill’, and δύο φῶτε is the dual ‘two men’. εἰδότε χάρμης ‘knowing the joy of battle’ has the dual perfect participle of οἶδα with the genitive of what is known; χάρμη is the delight of fighting. εἰν ἑνὶ δίφρῳ ἐόντε is ‘being in one chariot’ (εἰν is the epic form of ἐν, and ἐόντε the dual participle). Μενέσθην is Menesthes, not the Athenian leader Menestheus (Μενεσθεύς, 2.552), and Ἀγχίαλον is Anchialus.

sentences.t: τὼ δὲ πεσόντ’ ἐλέησε μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας·
sentences.tr: tō de pesont’ eleēse megas Telamōnios Aias·
sentences.l: And the two, fallen, pitied great Telamonian Ajax;
sentences.i: Great Telamonian Ajax pitied the two as they fell;
sentences.n: The first half of the line is the one said of Menelaus at 561, with Ajax now the one who pities. Τελαμώνιος is ‘Telamonian’, ‘son of Telamon’, the adjective that tells this Ajax from the son of Oileus, and μέγας is ‘great’. ἐλέησε is the aorist of ἐλεέω ‘pity’.

sentences.t:
στῆ δὲ μάλ’ ἐγγὺς ἰών, καὶ ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ,
καὶ βάλεν Ἄμφιον Σελάγου υἱόν, ὅς ῥ’ ἐνὶ Παισῷ
ναῖε πολυκτήμων πολυλήϊος·
sentences.tr:
stē de mal’ engys iōn, kai akontise douri phaeinōi,
kai balen Amphion Selagou huion, hos rh’ eni Paisōi
naie polyktēmōn polylēïos·
sentences.i: He took his stand very close and cast with his shining spear, and hit Amphius, the son of Selagus, who lived in Paesus, a man of many possessions and many cornfields;
sentences.n: The first line is the one said of Odysseus at 4.496 (the edition prints ἰών here and ἰὼν there), and its English is kept: στῆ is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι, and δουρὶ φαεινῷ is ‘with a shining spear’. Ἄμφιον is Amphius, and Σελάγου υἱόν is ‘son of Selagus’. Παισῷ is the dative of Παισός, the town Paesus, and ναῖε is the unaugmented imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’. πολυκτήμων is ‘of many possessions’ (κτῆμα) and πολυλήϊος ‘of many cornfields’ (λήϊον ‘standing grain, cornfield’).

sentences.t:
ἀλλά ἑ μοῖρα
ἦγ’ ἐπικουρήσοντα μετὰ Πρίαμόν τε καὶ υἷας.
sentences.tr:
alla he moira
ēg’ epikourēsonta meta Priamon te kai huias.
sentences.l:
but him fate
led, to help as an ally, to Priam and his sons.
sentences.i: but fate led him to be an ally to Priam and his sons.
sentences.n: ἑ is the pronoun ‘him’, and ἦγ’ is ἦγε, the imperfect of ἄγω. μοῖρα ‘fate’ is the subject. ἐπικουρήσοντα is the future participle of ἐπικουρέω, ‘to help as an ally’ (cf. ἐπίκουρος ‘ally’), expressing purpose, and μετὰ Πρίαμον … υἷας ‘to Priam and his sons’ takes μετά with the accusative of the goal (υἷας is the epic accusative plural of υἱός).

sentences.t:
τόν ῥα κατὰ ζωστῆρα βάλεν Τελαμώνιος Αἴας,
νειαίρῃ δ’ ἐν γαστρὶ πάγη δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος,
δούπησεν δὲ πεσών·
sentences.tr:
ton rha kata zōstēra balen Telamōnios Aias,
neiairēi d’ en gastri pagē dolichoskion enchos,
doupēsen de pesōn·
sentences.i: Telamonian Ajax hit him at the belt, and the long-shadowed spear was fixed in his lower belly, and he fell with a thud;
sentences.n: τόν ῥα ‘him, then’ is Amphius, and κατὰ ζωστῆρα is ‘at the belt’. The words νειαίρῃ δ’ ἐν γαστρί begin the line as they do at 539. πάγη is the aorist passive of πήγνυμι ‘fix’, and δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος ‘long-shadowed spear’ is the stock phrase. δούπησεν δὲ πεσών is the formula of 540, with its English.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐπέδραμε φαίδιμος Αἴας
τεύχεα συλήσων·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ epedrame phaidimos Aias
teuchea sylēsōn·
sentences.l:
and he ran up, glorious Ajax,
to strip the armour;
sentences.i: and glorious Ajax ran up to strip his armour;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is ‘and he’, with φαίδιμος Αἴας ‘glorious Ajax’ naming him; ἐπέδραμε is the aorist of ἐπιτρέχω ‘run up’. συλήσων is the future participle of συλάω ‘strip’, expressing purpose, and τεύχεα are the dead man’s ‘armour’.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δ’ ἐπὶ δούρατ’ ἔχευαν
ὀξέα παμφανόωντα·
sentences.tr:
Trōes d’ epi dourat’ echeuan
oxea pamphanoōnta·
sentences.l:
and the Trojans upon him poured spears,
sharp, all-shining;
sentences.i: and the Trojans poured sharp, all-shining spears upon him;
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … ἔχευαν is ‘poured upon’ (the English supplies ‘him’, Ajax), the preverb standing apart from the aorist of χέω, and δούρατ’ is δούρατα, the epic plural of δόρυ ‘spear’: the spears come as a shower. ὀξέα παμφανόωντα is ‘sharp, all-shining’ (παμφανόων is the epic participle form, and the Odyssey has the same word).

sentences.t: σάκος δ’ ἀνεδέξατο πολλά.
sentences.tr: sakos d’ anedexato polla.
sentences.l: and the shield received many.
sentences.i: and his shield took many of them.
sentences.n: σάκος ‘shield’ is the subject and ἀνεδέξατο, the aorist middle of ἀναδέχομαι, is ‘received, took up’. πολλά is ‘many’, neuter plural for the spears of the unit before.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ λὰξ προσβὰς ἐκ νεκροῦ χάλκεον ἔγχος
ἐσπάσατ’·
sentences.tr:
autar ho lax prosbas ek nekrou chalkeon enchos
espasat’·
sentences.l:
but he, stepping on it with his heel, out of the corpse the bronze spear
drew;
sentences.i: But he set his heel on the body and drew the bronze spear out of it;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ is ‘but he’, Ajax. λάξ is ‘with the heel’, and προσβάς, the aorist participle of προσβαίνω, ‘stepping on’ the body. ἐκ νεκροῦ is ‘out of the corpse’, and χάλκεον ἔγχος ‘the bronze spear’ is his own spear, which was fixed in the belly at 616. ἐσπάσατ’ is ἐσπάσατο, the aorist middle of σπάω ‘draw’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτ’ ἄλλα δυνήσατο τεύχεα καλὰ
ὤμοιιν ἀφελέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ar’ et’ alla dynēsato teuchea kala
ōmoiin aphelesthai·
sentences.l:
nor then any longer was he able the other fine armour
from the two shoulders to take off;
sentences.i: and he could no longer take the rest of the fine armour from his shoulders;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτ’ ἄλλα is ‘nor then any longer the other things’, the rest of the armour (τεύχεα καλά ‘fine armour’), so only the spear came away. δυνήσατο is the aorist middle of δύναμαι ‘be able’. ὤμοιιν is a dual genitive, ‘from the two shoulders’, and ἀφελέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ἀφαιρέω ‘take off’.

sentences.t: ἐπείγετο γὰρ βελέεσσι.
sentences.tr: epeigeto gar beleessi.
sentences.l: for he was pressed hard with shafts.
sentences.i: for he was hard pressed by their shafts.
sentences.n: ἐπείγετο is the imperfect passive of ἐπείγω ‘press hard’, and γάρ gives the reason he could not strip the body. βελέεσσι is the epic dative plural of βέλος ‘shaft’, the missile; ‘their’ is supplied from the Trojans of 618.

sentences.t:
δεῖσε δ’ ὅ γ’ ἀμφίβασιν κρατερὴν Τρώων ἀγερώχων,
οἳ πολλοί τε καὶ ἐσθλοὶ ἐφέστασαν ἔγχε’ ἔχοντες,
οἵ ἑ μέγαν περ ἐόντα καὶ ἴφθιμον καὶ ἀγαυὸν
ὦσαν ἀπὸ σφείων·
sentences.tr:
deise d’ ho g’ amphibasin kraterēn Trōōn agerōchōn,
hoi polloi te kai esthloi ephestasan enche’ echontes,
hoi he megan per eonta kai iphthimon kai agauon
ōsan apo spheiōn·
sentences.l:
And he feared the strong circle of the lofty Trojans,
who many and good stood about him holding spears,
who him, great though he was, and mighty, and noble,
pushed away from themselves;
sentences.i: He was afraid of the strong ring of the lofty Trojans, who, many and good, stood about him holding spears, and who pushed him away from them, great though he was, and mighty and noble;
sentences.n: δεῖσε is the aorist of δείδω ‘fear’, taking an accusative. ἀμφίβασιν is the accusative of ἀμφίβασις, a rare noun built on ἀμφιβαίνω ‘step round’, here the ring of men standing about a fallen man to guard him; κρατερήν is ‘strong’. Τρώων ἀγερώχων ‘of the lofty Trojans’: ἀγέρωχος is a stock epithet of the Trojans, a word whose meaning is not known. ἐφέστασαν is the pluperfect of ἐφίστημι ‘had taken their stand over’. The last two lines are 4.534–535, said there of Thoas, and their English is kept: περ with ἐόντα is ‘though he was’, ἴφθιμον ‘mighty’, ἀγαυόν ‘noble’, and ὦσαν the aorist of ὠθέω ‘push’, with σφείων the epic genitive plural ‘them’.

sentences.t: ὃ δὲ χασσάμενος πελεμίχθη.
sentences.tr: ho de chassamenos pelemichthē.
sentences.l: and he, having given ground, was shaken.
sentences.i: and he gave ground, reeling.
sentences.n: ὃ δὲ is Ajax here. The line is the second half of 4.535, and its English is kept: χασσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of χάζομαι ‘give ground’, and πελεμίχθη the aorist passive of πελεμίζω ‘shake, make reel’.
